extracted.intended_audience: general readers and YouTube content creators / policy stakeholders
extracted.subtask_short: youtube content policy and monetization guidelines
extracted.subtask_description: Platform-level criteria and eligibility rules for YouTube features, monetization, content restrictions, and censorship/privacy issues as described in the article. Covers feature eligibility (Stories/Shorts/YouTube Kids), monetization thresholds and revenue sharing, advertiser-friendly content rules, and reasons/grounds for removals or state bans.

rubrics_metrics.name: YouTube Kids content curation
rubrics_metrics.description: The app provides a version of the service oriented towards children, with curated selections of content, parental control features, and filtering of videos deemed inappropriate viewing for children aged under 13, 8 or 5, depending on the age grouping chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to respond to parental and government scrutiny; available as Android/iOS apps and on many smart TVs and web (launched Feb 15, 2015; web-based version launched Aug 30, 2019). The article notes this is the intended approach rather than a precise algorithm; no detailed filtering rules are given on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: YouTube Shorts length & creative-tool constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Shorts was launched as a platform of 15-second videos (later allowing up to 1 minute), integrated into the main YouTube app and offering built-in creative tools including the possibility of adding licensed music. On October 15, 2024 the platform officially extended the length of shorts to 3 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorts is not a standalone app (initially tested in India, global beta July 13, 2021). Creators should use the built-in tools and licensed-music features when preparing short-form content; the page documents historical length limits and tool availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: YouTube Stories eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube Stories (originally 'YouTube Reels') was nearly identical to Instagram/Snapchat Stories and was only available to creators who had more than 10,000 subscribers and could only be posted/seen in the YouTube mobile app.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was a gated feature (subscriber threshold) and was later shut down (announced May 25, 2023; shut down June 26, 2023). Feature eligibility here is an example of subscriber-based access controls for creator features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility requirements for monetization / Partner Program / paid subscriptions (historical and current)
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube changed eligibility rules over time: on April 6, 2017 YouTube required that a channel undergo a policy compliance review and have at least 10,000-lifetime views before they may join the YouTube Partner Program; on January 16, 2018 the eligibility requirement for monetization was changed to 4,000 hours of watch-time within the past 12 months and 1,000 subscribers. Paid-subscription eligibility has also changed (channels with at least a thousand subscribers could require a paid subscription in 2013; in April 2017 YouTube set an eligibility requirement of 10,000 lifetime views for a paid subscription).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These thresholds were introduced to "ensure revenue only flows to creators who are playing by the rules" but were criticized for penalizing smaller channels. Creators preparing to monetize must meet the applicable historical/current thresholds and pass policy compliance reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser-friendly content restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube's policies restrict certain forms of content from being included in videos being monetized with advertising, including videos containing violence, strong language, sexual content, and "controversial or sensitive subjects and events, including subjects related to war, political conflicts, natural disasters and tragedies, even if graphic imagery is not shown" (unless the content is "usually newsworthy or comedic and the creator intends to inform or entertain").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: YouTube has implemented enhanced notification and appeal processes to inform users of violations. The policy has been controversial among creators (criticisms from Philip DeFranco, Vlogbrothers, reports of LGBT keywords resulting in demonetization). Creators should consider intent (newsworthy/comedic/informative) and be prepared to appeal takedowns or demonetization where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization affected by user comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Videos whose user comments contain "inappropriate" content may be restricted from being monetized with advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators should moderate comments and community behavior; presence of inappropriate comments can impact a video's eligibility for ads even if the video content itself meets advertiser-friendly standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: YouTube's right to monetize non-Partner videos
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube reserves the right to monetize any video on the platform, even if their uploader is not a member of the YouTube Partner Program. When this occurs, all revenue will go directly to Google without any share given to the uploader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of November 2020 in the U.S. and June 2021 worldwide, this policy allows YouTube to place ads on content from non-YPP creators; creators should be aware they may not receive ad revenue even if ads appear on their videos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue split for Partner Program members
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube typically takes 45 percent of the advertising revenue from videos in the Partner Program, with 55 percent going to the uploader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the stated revenue-sharing arrangement for videos in the YPP; the page also notes there are over two million YPP members and historical context about ad pricing and revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: YouTube Creator Rewards (Play Buttons) thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube Play Buttons are given to channels with at least one hundred thousand, a million, ten million, fifty million, and one hundred million subscribers, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trophies are made of various materials (nickel-plated copper-nickel alloy, golden-plated brass, silver-plated metal, ruby, and red-tinted crystal glass) and serve as recognition milestones for creators.

rubrics_metrics.name: State censorship / reasons for blocking YouTube
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube has been censored, filtered, or banned for reasons including: limiting public access and exposure to content that may ignite social or political unrest; preventing criticism of a ruler, government, or religion; morality-based laws; copyright and intellectual property protections; violations of hate speech rules; and preventing access to videos judged inappropriate for youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blocks may be nationwide or temporary (e.g., during unrest or elections). The article gives many country examples (China, North Korea, Iran, Pakistan, Turkey, Thailand, Morocco, Libya, Pakistan again) and notes that in some cases YouTube will remove or limit access to a video to restore service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content removal in response to government policy or sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube has removed channels and videos following government policy decisions and sanctions (for example, removal of RT from the platform in Europe following the Russian invasion of Ukraine and expansion globally; removal of accounts and videos of several Palestinian human rights organizations in 2025 to comply with U.S. sanctions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform compliance with governmental orders or sanctions can lead to removal of newsworthy or human-rights-related material; the article documents specific incidents and dates as examples of how geopolitical/legal pressures affect content availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy and child-data collection concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Since founding, YouTube has faced allegations that it allows users to upload unauthorized copyrighted material and allows personal information from young children to be collected without their parents' consent. A September 2024 FTC report summarizing company responses found that user and non-user data practices put individuals vulnerable to identity theft, stalking, unlawful discrimination, emotional distress and mental health issues, social stigma, and reputational harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These regulatory concerns have led to scrutiny and requests for information under Section 6(b) of the FTC Act; creators and platform operators should be aware of privacy obligations and potential regulatory consequences.
